53412.etyen:
Borrowed from Middle Low German schonrogge (“white, light rye”), also schonerogge, literally “beautiful (light, white) rye”, from schōne (“beautiful; fair, light”) and rogge (“rye”).
First attested in 1793 in Norwegian customs records, in a Vardø import list recording 700 pounds of “Brød, Skonrok” imported from Denmark.
Compare Old Danish skonroggen, Old Swedish skanroggä and Icelandic skonrok (“large rusk, biscuit”).

1000100.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from the name of the Senegal River; compare French Sénégal. The country takes its name from the river.
The origin of the river name is uncertain. One common explanation connects it with Azenegue, a Portuguese name for the Zenaga or Sanhaja, a Berber group that lived north of the river. Fifteenth-century Portuguese accounts record related ethnonym forms such as Azanaghi, Azenegues, Cenegii and Azaneguys; modern Zenaga speakers call themselves Iznāgen. The deeper origin of the ethnonym and the exact development from it to the river name remain uncertain.

1001380.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Guðrún, through a younger Norwegian form in which the final /n/ was lost after nasalising the preceding vowel. The Old Norse name is from guð (“god”) + rún (“secret knowledge, rune”).
Doublet of Gudrun (“female given name”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Guro, Danish Guro, Swedish Guro, Icelandic Guðrún and Faroese Guðrun (“female given name”).

1003172.etyen:
From the suffixal use of verdig (“worthy; fitting”), inherited from verðugr (“worthy”), derived from verðr (“worthy; worth”). In some formations, -verdig replaced older -verd under the influence of German -würdig (“-worthy”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -verdig, Danish -værdig, Swedish -värdig, German -würdig, Dutch -waardig and English -worthy (“adjective-forming suffix”).

1004708.etyen:
Possibly from Old Norse Herjulfssetr, from the male given name Herjulfr + setr (“farmstead, dwelling”), literally “Herjulfr’s farmstead”. The proposed derivation is uncertain. The second element setr is from Proto-Germanic *setrą (“seat, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).
Compare other Norwegian farm names in -set.
